result:
CORS is enforced by the browser, not the server. curl isn't a browser: no same-origin policy, so it never checks. Your server likely answers fine in both cases; the browser just refuses to hand the response to JS because it lacks `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` matching the page's origin.

Second common cause: preflight. Non-"simple" requests (`Content-Type: application/json`, `Authorization` or custom headers, PUT/DELETE/PATCH) → browser sends `OPTIONS` first. Server 404s/401s/redirects it or omits the allow headers → real request never sent. curl skips preflight entirely.

Reproduce what the browser sees:

```bash
curl -i -X OPTIONS https://api.example.com/path \
  -H 'Origin: https://your-site.com' \
  -H 'Access-Control-Request-Method: POST' \
  -H 'Access-Control-Request-Headers: content-type,authorization'
```

Need 2xx plus `Access-Control-Allow-Origin`, `-Allow-Methods`, `-Allow-Headers` covering what you asked for.

Fix is server-side: return those headers (most frameworks have CORS middleware), or serve the API same-origin via a reverse/dev proxy so CORS never applies. Nothing in frontend code can fix it; `mode: 'no-cors'` only gives an opaque, unreadable response.

Gotchas: with cookies/`credentials: 'include'`, `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` is rejected → echo the exact origin plus `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true`. Error responses (500s, auth failures) often skip the CORS middleware → real bug shows up as a CORS error; check the Network tab status.

CORS doesn't protect the server: simple requests still arrive and execute, only the read is blocked. Not a substitute for auth/CSRF.
